# Writing Style: Textbook (Giáo Trình)

Sources: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 & Introduction to Sociology 3e (live, Apr 2026); Anderson & Krathwohl (2001) *A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing*; Mayer (2001) *Multimedia Learning*, Cambridge UP; Sweller (1988) Cognitive Load Theory; Wiggins & McTighe (1998) *Understanding by Design*; ADB Technical Assistance Report 42079 (Vietnam HE).

---

## Core Philosophy

Textbook writing **teaches**, not informs. Every sentence serves a learner who is encountering this concept for the first time. The writer's job is to reduce cognitive load, build schema, and motivate the reader to keep going.

Three principles govern everything:
- **Commitment** — state definitions clearly and directly, no hedging
- **Scaffolding** — introduce complexity in controlled doses, one concept at a time
- **Motivation** — connect abstract concepts to real situations before diving in

The register sits between research paper (too hedged, assumes expertise) and professional memo (too terse, no teaching intent). The reader is a student, addressed as **"you"**.

---

## 1. Chapter & Section Architecture

Every chapter follows this canonical structure (verified: OpenStax, Pearson, McGraw-Hill):

```
Opening Image + Motivating Caption
Chapter Outline (section links)
Chapter Introduction (1–3 paragraphs, narrative hook — no headings)
  ├── Section N.1
  │    ├── Learning Objectives
  │    ├── Prose body with callout boxes
  │    └── Check Your Understanding
  ├── Section N.2 ... (repeats)
Chapter Summary
Key Terms (glossary)
Review Questions (conceptual)
Problems / Exercises (tiered difficulty)
```

**Vietnamese Giáo Trình variant** — add these structural elements:
- **Lời nói đầu / Lời mở đầu** (Preface): 1–2 pages, states purpose, scope, target audience, institutional context
- **Mục tiêu chương** (Chapter objectives): numbered list before content
- **Tóm tắt** (Summary): end of chapter
- **Câu hỏi ôn tập** (Review questions): end of chapter
- **Tài liệu tham khảo** (References): end of book
- Numbered definitions: **Định nghĩa N.M:** and numbered examples: **Ví dụ N.M:**
- Formal approval framing in front matter

---

## 2. Learning Objectives (LOs) — The Non-Negotiable First Element

Every section opens with **3–5 learning objectives** before any prose. These are the contract with the reader.

**Format:**
> By the end of this section, you will be able to:
> - [Bloom's verb] [specific, measurable outcome]
> - [Bloom's verb] [specific, measurable outcome]

**Bloom's verb table** (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) — match verb level to where in the chapter:

| Level | Verbs | Use in |
|---|---|---|
| Remember | define, list, identify, recall, name | Early sections |
| Understand | explain, describe, summarize, interpret | Core body |
| Apply | calculate, solve, use, demonstrate | Worked examples |
| Analyze | compare, differentiate, examine, distinguish | End-of-section questions |
| Evaluate | justify, critique, assess, defend | Challenge problems |
| Create | design, construct, formulate, develop | Projects/capstone |

**Rule:** The Bloom's level of each LO must match the Bloom's level of the corresponding review question. If you write "describe X" as an LO, the review question must ask them to describe, not design.

---

## 3. Concept Introduction — The DEFA Pattern

For every new concept, follow this sequence (derived from Cognitive Load Theory, Sweller 1988):

```
1. DEFINE   — "[Term] is [definition in plain language]." Bold the term. Commit.
2. EXAMPLE  — Concrete, relatable, everyday. "Consider a smartphone..."
3. FIGURE   — Visual or worked example. Caption repeats the key point.
4. ASSESS   — "Check Your Understanding" question targeting the specific LO just taught.
```

**STEM variant:** Define → Equation → Worked Example → Check (DEEC)
**Social science variant:** Claim → Evidence → Contextualization → Critical question (CECC)

**Key rule (Mayer's Spatial Contiguity Principle):** The figure and its explanation must appear on the same page. Never put a figure three paragraphs away from the text that discusses it.

---

## 4. Prose Style Rules

### Definitions — Commit, Don't Hedge
| ❌ Research paper | ✅ Textbook |
|---|---|
| "X can be understood as approximately Y in certain conditions" | "**X** is Y." |
| "Scholars have debated the meaning of Z, with Foucault suggesting..." | "**Z** is [definition]. Scholars disagree on [one specific point], but in this course we use [working definition]." |

**Rule:** Bold the term on first use. Use "is" not "can be" or "may refer to."

### Voice — Second Person, Active
| ❌ | ✅ |
|---|---|
| "The student will encounter entropy in thermodynamics." | "In this section, **you will** learn to calculate entropy changes." |
| "It was shown that price increases reduce demand." | "When prices rise, **you** generally buy less — that's the law of demand." |

### Sentence Length — Medium Register
- Target 15–25 words per sentence
- Vary rhythm: short assertion → longer explanation → short summary
- No embedded relative clauses that delay the main verb past word 12

### New Terms — Controlled Dosing (Cognitive Load)
- **One new technical term per ~2 paragraphs** — never pre-load a list of 8 definitions before context
- Introduce a term only when the prose immediately needs it
- Every bolded term must be in the Key Terms glossary at the end of the chapter

---

## 5. Callout Box Taxonomy

Use named boxes consistently. Minimum required set:

| Box | Purpose | Format |
|---|---|---|
| **Learning Objectives** | Opens every section | "By the end of this section, you will be able to:" + bulleted Bloom-verbs |
| **Definition** | Formal definition of a key term | Bold heading = the term; body = definition |
| **Example / Worked Example** | Numbered, step-by-step | Strategy → Steps → Check |
| **Check Your Understanding** | Immediate retrieval practice | 1–2 questions after a concept, matching the LO |
| **Key Takeaway** | Distills the section's core claim | 1–3 sentences max |
| **Real-World Application** | Connects abstract to profession/life | "In a hospital setting…", "When you file your taxes…" |
| **Did You Know? / Interesting Note** | Biographical/historical context, builds curiosity | Anecdote, not trivia |
| **Common Misconception** | Flags known student errors before they form | "Students often think X, but actually Y because Z." |

**Vietnamese equivalents:**
- Định nghĩa / Khái niệm (Definition)
- Ví dụ (Example)
- Nhận xét / Chú ý (Note/Remark)
- Định lý / Hệ quả (Theorem/Corollary — math/science)
- Tóm tắt (Key Takeaway)
- Ứng dụng thực tế (Real-World Application)

---

## 6. Chapter Hook — Never Start with the Abstract

Every chapter (and ideally every major section) opens with a **hook before any concept**:
- A compelling image with a motivating caption
- A 1–3 paragraph narrative: a real scenario, historical moment, or "you've probably encountered this" situation
- The hook answers the implicit question: *"Why should I care about this?"*

**❌ Bad opening:**
> "This chapter covers molecular orbital theory."

**✅ OpenStax-style opening:**
> [Image of aurora borealis]
> "On a clear night above the Arctic Circle, ribbons of green and violet light dance across the sky. These northern lights—the aurora borealis—are caused by electrons from the sun colliding with atoms in Earth's upper atmosphere. To understand exactly why each element produces a specific color, you need molecular orbital theory."

The hook creates a **knowledge gap** the student wants to close. Then you deliver the concept.

---

## 7. Before/After Examples

### Topic: Inflation

**❌ Academic paper:**
> "The phenomenon of inflation, broadly conceived as a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, has been examined across multiple econometric frameworks, with empirical studies suggesting causal mechanisms including monetary policy decisions, supply-side constraints, and demand-pull dynamics (Fisher, 1911; Friedman, 1963)."

Problems: hedged, assumes prior vocabulary, passive, no student orientation.

**✅ Textbook:**
> **Inflation** is a sustained increase in the overall price level of goods and services in an economy. When inflation occurs, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services than it did before.
>
> Consider a loaf of bread that costs $2 today. If it costs $2.10 next year, its price rose by 5%—that is inflation at work. Inflation affects everyone: a retiree on a fixed pension loses purchasing power, while a business owner must charge more just to cover rising input costs. Understanding inflation will help you make better financial decisions throughout your life.

---

### Topic: Social Norms

**❌ Research paper:**
> "Social norms, operationalized as collectively shared behavioral standards that members of a group are expected to conform to (Cialdini & Trost, 1998), vary significantly across cultural contexts and are enforced through informal sanctioning mechanisms."

**✅ Textbook:**
> A **social norm** is an unwritten rule that members of a group follow. Norms tell us how to behave in social situations. Some are obvious—most people in a restaurant don't shout across the room. Others are subtle—in some cultures, making eye contact shows respect; in others, it can signal aggression.
>
> When someone violates a norm, others often react with discomfort or disapproval. Sociologists call this **informal sanctioning**—social pressure that enforces norms without any formal law or rule. This is why running through a library feels different from running through a park, even though neither is illegal.

---

## 8. Failure Modes (Do Not Do These)

| Failure | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition dumping** | 10 terms defined before any context | One new term per ~2 paragraphs, only when needed |
| **Invisible reader** | Passive voice, third-person throughout | "You will learn…", direct second person |
| **Unmotivated abstract** | Chapter opens with the concept, not the hook | Image + scenario + knowledge gap first |
| **Fake worked examples** | Shows steps without explaining *why* | Add "Strategy" block before each worked example |
| **Wall of prose** | 4+ paragraphs with no visual break | Bold subheadings, callout boxes, lists |
| **LO/exercise mismatch** | LO says "describe", exam asks to "design" | Align Bloom's level end-to-end |
| **Authority-only tone** (Vietnamese) | "Sinh viên phải nắm..." with no motivation | Add real-world connection after every major concept |

---

## 9. Pre-Publish Checklist

- [ ] Every section has a **Learning Objectives** block with Bloom's-level verbs
- [ ] Every new term is **bolded** on first use and listed in Key Terms
- [ ] No more than 1 new term introduced per ~2 paragraphs
- [ ] Every section has at least one **Check Your Understanding** question
- [ ] Bloom's level of LOs matches Bloom's level of review questions
- [ ] Every figure has a caption that restates the key point
- [ ] Figures appear on the same page as their explanatory text
- [ ] Chapter/section opens with a hook before any abstract concept
- [ ] Prose uses second person ("you") and active voice throughout
- [ ] Required callout boxes present: Definition, Example, Key Takeaway, Check Your Understanding
- [ ] (Vietnamese) Includes Lời nói đầu, Mục tiêu, Tóm tắt, Câu hỏi ôn tập
